idiom_name: module facade with `module_function`; stdlib Forwardable for generated delegation
implementation_notes: A Ruby facade is usually a small class or a module: module_function turns the curated methods into both module-level entry points and private instance methods, which is exactly the narrow surface a facade wants. When the facade forwards many methods verbatim, the standard library's Forwardable (def_delegators :@client, :get, :post) or DelegateClass generates the delegation instead of hand-written wrappers. Keep unexposed subsystem classes namespaced or private to the library; Ruby has no package-private, so the module boundary plus naming discipline is the hiding mechanism.
code_sketch:
module Media                       # module facade: one entry point
  module_function

  def convert(file, target)
    AudioMixer.fix(CodecFactory.convert(file, target))
  end
end
Media.convert("clip.ogg", "mp4")
pitfalls: module_function privately copies the methods into the module's singleton and makes the instance copies private; mixing the module in and expecting public methods surprises people.
method_missing-based delegation hides the real API from readers and tools; prefer explicit def_delegators lists.
Monkey-patching collaborators from inside a facade leaks into every client of the process; keep refinements and explicit APIs instead.
Ruby's open classes mean the private-ish constants can still be reached; treat the facade as a documented contract, not an enforcement point.
